source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Defines epistemic action: a physical action whose main job is to improve the agent's own cognition, not to move it closer to the goal. Pragmatic action is the opposite. The paper argues from Tetris data that classic models cannot explain many 'superfluous' moves.
numbers: Three claimed benefits: less memory (space), fewer steps (time), lower error probability (unreliability).
quote: actions performed to uncover information that is hidden or hard to compute mentally
limits: Definition is functional, so one action can be both epistemic and pragmatic; the authors admit this makes quantifying hard.
agent_relevance: Maps to an agent tool call whose purpose is to reveal information (probe, print, run on a toy input) rather than advance the answer. Gives three measurable payoffs to score probes against: tokens, steps, error rate.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Paradigm: players of Tetris on a 10 by 30 board with 7 zoids and only 4 actions (rotate 90 deg, move left, move right, drop). Fall speed rises with score. Three data sources: keystroke and game-state logs from a computational lab, tachistoscopic mental rotation tests, and RoboTetris, an expert system used as a classical comparison.
numbers: Free fall about 200 ms per square at start to about 100 ms at the maximum. A newcomer reaches intermediate level in under 10 hours. Shortest inter-keystroke interval about 75 ms; average about 250 ms.
limits: Number of participants and total episodes for the main logs is not stated in the article text I read. No controlled manipulation of epistemic action; evidence is observational plus interpretation.
agent_relevance: Tetris is a good lab because every action is deterministic and cheap, similar to a code probe with no side effects.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: The classical foil: a four-phase serial model (bitmap, chunked encoding, choose placement, compute motor plan). Under it, any action made before the plan is done should be random. Relaxing it to a cascade or interleaved planner still fails.
numbers: If players plan first, a 4-orientation zoid should average 1.5 rotations (half of the 3 possible). Observed: every zoid type was rotated more than half its possible rotations (Fig. 6, 95% CIs; exact bar values are not in the text). Rotations begin in earnest at 400 to 600 ms and sometimes before 100 ms.
limits: Bar heights are only in a figure; the text gives no per-zoid means.
agent_relevance: Shows why an agent that only counts 'progress steps' will wrongly judge exploratory calls as waste.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Why false starts do not explain the extra rotations: a false start costs 75 to 750 ms to undo, and some rotations happen before the shape is even fully visible. Players are bad at estimating the final orientation that early, so acting on that estimate would be unwise. The better reading is that early rotation reveals information.
numbers: Recovery from over-rotation takes 1 to 3 extra rotations, 75 to 750 ms.
limits: Argument by exclusion; no direct test of intent.
agent_relevance: Cheap, reversible probes can beat waiting for a confident plan when the probe cost is a fraction of the recovery cost.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Epistemic use 1, early rotation for discovery: rotating an emerging zoid exposes its hidden part 150 to 300 ms earlier than waiting. Players rotate more when the partial image is ambiguous in both shape and column. Partly visible zoids ambiguous in shape alone (column disambiguates) are not rotated more than unambiguous ones.
numbers: At medium speed one square per 150 ms, so a full zoid takes about half a second to appear. Players use column information without being able to report it in interviews.
quote: no player reported noticing that zoids begin falling in different columns
limits: The ambiguity contrast is described but exact rates are in a figure; no test values in the text.
agent_relevance: Evidence that probing is sensitive to real information value, even implicitly. A probe policy should fire when the current view is ambiguous, not on a schedule (fits G1).

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Epistemic use 2, saving mental rotation effort: physical rotation takes far less time than mental rotation, so rotate in the world and compare. A pilot with three players (intermediate, advanced, expert) did a Shepard and Metzler style same/mirror task on S and L zoids; reaction time rose linearly with angle difference.
numbers: 3 players; 8 presentations per pair type; RT about 0.6 to 1.3 s over 0 to 180 deg (read off the Fig. 10 axis). Estimated mental rotation of 90 deg: 800 to 1200 ms vs physical 100 ms (+200 ms to choose the key). No flat line seen even for experts.
limits: Very small pilot (N=3), only correct 'same' trials plotted, the 800 to 1200 ms figure is an estimate. A later paper (Kirsh 1995) quotes 1000 to 1800 ms, so the number is soft.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue: do a cheap external computation (run code, enumerate) instead of simulating it in text, when the external step is 5 to 10 times faster and less error prone.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Epistemic uses 3 to 5 are mechanism proposals, not tested: rotation as a second retrieval cue (a Boltzmann-machine style attractor settles faster with two cues), rotation to shrink an attention decision tree from depth 3 to depth 2, and rotation to let perception do matching so that mental imagery need not be refreshed every 200 ms.
numbers: Illustration only: 1200 ms with one view vs 1000 ms with two views is a conjecture ('ripe for experimental testing'). Decision tree: at most 3 probes without rotation, at most 2 with rotation.
limits: Explicitly untested conjectures; the authors say it is an open question whether players hold multi-view representations.
agent_relevance: Gives candidate mechanisms for why viewing an input in a second form (diff, table, sorted) helps; test each as an O6 hypothesis, not as a fact.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Epistemic use 6, translate-to-wall verification: in about 1% of drops, players first move the zoid to the nearest wall and back, then drop. This is pragmatically useless and is used more when the drop is higher, where column judgement is least accurate.
numbers: Table 1 mean drop distance (squares), ordinary drop vs translate-routine drop: intermediate 13.18 vs 19.04; advanced 13.69 vs 19.33; expert 15.65 vs 20.05. Each pair differs by t test at alpha .05. Fig. 15: share of verified drops rises with drop height.
quote: the higher the drop, the more likely it followed a verification routine
limits: Only about 1% of drops; observed associations, no randomised control; skill-group sizes not given in the text.
agent_relevance: Strong cost-benefit signature: verification is bought exactly where error risk is highest. Supports risk-triggered checks (G3) over fixed-schedule checks.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Formal framing: planning as state-space search must use states that pair physical state with informational state, so an action sequence that returns the board to its start can still change what the agent knows. The payoff of an action has two parts, physical and epistemic, in a cost-benefit model like Stigler's economics of information.
numbers: No numeric model fitted. The authors say the value of an epistemic action depends on the agent's internal processes (the value of a rotation at 500 ms depends on the current cognitive state), so generic value-of-information formulas are not enough.
limits: No computational model with fitted parameters was produced; the claim that expected epistemic value needs a model of the agent's own cognition remains open.
agent_relevance: For an LLM agent the 'informational state' can be made explicit: the set of facts verified so far. A probe is worth running if it changes that set.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Novel claim about skill: experts do not only cache or chunk faster routines; they learn qualitatively different tricks (expose information early, prime recognition, verify externally). This is set against chunking and caching accounts of skill (Newell and Rosenbloom; Logan).
quote: Agents do not simply cache associative rules describing what to do
limits: Argument from observation; the 1996 paper supplies longitudinal data for only two players.
agent_relevance: Suggests an agent should learn when to probe, not just speed up its direct attempts.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Generalisation offered beyond Tetris: novice chess players move pieces to see replies, advanced players change viewpoint to break set, people shuffle, annotate and perturb the world to jog memory or shatter presuppositions. The paper claims epistemic action holds 'throughout all of human activity'.
limits: Only Tetris has data in this paper; the rest is illustration and citation.
agent_relevance: Perturbing the input (reorder, rename, mutate) is the agent version of changing viewpoint to break fixation.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (c. 1992, year not printed) Perceptive Actions in Tetris
finding: Earlier four-page workshop version (pp. 86-89 of a proceedings; scanned, read as page images). Argues three ways to regulate information intake: control attention, control gaze, control activity. Tetris is the testbed for the third. Three phenomena: rotate in midstream, rotate early, translate to verify.
numbers: Data from 30 subjects playing Tetris is mentioned. Hypothesis that a left-handed L is rotated to match a mirror 'natural receptor' contour to verify fit. No statistics given.
limits: Qualitative, no numbers or tests in the text; a short symposium paper; year inferred.
agent_relevance: Shows the idea began as a perception and attention story, close to selective information intake, before it became an action-theory claim.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1992) Reaction and Reflection in Tetris (in Hendler (Ed.) AI planning systems)
finding: RoboTetris: a skill-based player using 6 board features (holes, total height, mountain height, covered holes, filled rows, local fitness) with a weighted sum. Weights can beat any human, but its behaviour is unlike humans: too consistent in score, odd peaks. Proposed that a reflective layer should bias attention input rather than override outputs.
numbers: State space about 17 x 2^270 in principle; 6 features used.
limits: Short two-page chapter; no human comparison numbers in the pages read.
agent_relevance: Design hint: a higher-level monitor that changes what the agent looks at (input) may work better than one that vetoes its answers (output).

source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) Epistemic action increases with skill (CogSci 18)
finding: First longitudinal test. Two novices practised Tetris about 20 hours each (about 40,000 keystrokes). Speed followed the power law of practice, yet backtracking (actions off the shortest path) increased with skill. This contradicts the common assumption that experts make fewer redundant moves.
numbers: N = 2 players (LA reported in detail, TM in a thesis). Extra rotations in 7% of expert episodes, 5% intermediate, 4% beginner (p about .01); mean about 0.2 extra rotations per episode. Slow episodes only, three 6-hour bins.
quote: as skill increases, the proportion of game actions that are later undone by backtracking also increases
limits: N=2 and a small absolute rate (about 0.2 per episode). Most detail is for one player. Our SUBFIELDS note says a follow-up found these actions DECLINE with expertise; the primary paper read here says the opposite (increase), so that note needs checking.
agent_relevance: Counter to the intuition that a skilled agent needs fewer steps. A good scaffold may spend more cheap probes as it gets better, as long as total time falls.

source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) Epistemic action increases with skill
finding: Speed-up still followed a power law: for time between actions, power fits beat linear and exponential fits for both players, following Newell and Rosenbloom's method.
numbers: Time between actions, r squared: LA linear .7721, exponential .8439, power .9108; TM linear .8117, exponential .8789, power .9557. 38 data points per player (30-min blocks). Time to place a zoid, LA: .7711 / .8020 / .8306 (linear / exp / power).
limits: Two-parameter fits chosen to avoid overfitting 38 points; r squared differences are modest for time of first action (LA .7234 vs .7515).
agent_relevance: Epistemic actions did not slow the net learning curve, so extra probing was net-neutral or positive for speed.

source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) Epistemic action increases with skill
finding: Ruled out error explanations for extra rotations. Motor slips would hit all zoid types equally, but extra rotations varied by zoid type. Perceptual confusion with mirror images would raise them in mirror episodes, but mirror and non-mirror rates did not differ.
numbers: Mirror vs non-mirror: no significant difference at any skill level (chi square, p above .05 reported as 'in all cases').
limits: The mirror test is a null result on a rare event (about 4 to 7% of episodes), so power may be low.
agent_relevance: Good example of how to separate 'probe' from 'mistake': check whether it varies with information value, not randomly.

source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) Epistemic action increases with skill
finding: Timing evidence: extra rotations occur when the zoid reaches its final orientation early (before the player has decided), consistent with rotating to help the decision. Extra-rotation episodes reached the target orientation earlier.
numbers: Mean time to final orientation with vs without extra rotations: 676 vs 1127 ms (SD 149, 99; t(198)=2.82, p=.005) for one zoid type; 754 vs 1122 ms (SD 296, 71; t(293)=2.24, p=.026) for the other. Player LA, slow episodes, expert level.
limits: One player, two zoid types, post hoc; alternative: early arrival simply gives more time to fiddle.
agent_relevance: Probe when you are early or idle: if the cheap hypothesis is already on screen, extra looks cost little.

source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) Epistemic action increases with skill
finding: Interpretation: the world acts as an interactive visuo-spatial sketchpad, not a passive memory. Eye movements change input without changing the task; a rotation changes input and the task, so it does more work.
quote: the external world functions ... more like a working memory system, that is, like an interactive visuo-spatial sketchpad
limits: Conceptual claim; no model fitted.
agent_relevance: Our tool outputs can be treated as working memory that the model rewrites, not just logs.

source: Kirsh (1995) Complementary strategies: why we use our hands when we think (CogSci 17)
finding: Defines complementary strategies (broader than epistemic action): any organising activity that recruits external elements to cut cognitive load, such as pointing, arranging, writing. Pilot coin-counting study: hands allowed vs not allowed.
numbers: N = 5 (3 male, 2 female, 23 to 38 years). 30 coin images per condition (21 to 31 coins, mean 26). Time 22.5 s no-hands vs 18.7 s hands. Errors 68% (20.3 of 30) vs 42% (12.6 of 30). Per-subject p < .04 for time and errors; the aggregate p values in the text read 'p<.4', apparently a typo.
limits: Pilot, N=5, same images in both conditions, order effects possible; text has inconsistent p values. Subjects experimented with techniques in about the first 20% of trials, then settled.
agent_relevance: A simple external aid cut errors by about 40% (relative) even in a trivial task. Supports cheap structure (tallies, marks) in the scaffold.

source: Kirsh (1995) The intelligent use of space (Artificial Intelligence 73)
finding: Review that places epistemic action in a taxonomy of how agents structure workspaces: simplify choice, simplify perception, simplify internal computation. Restates Tetris numbers and adds self-cueing (shuffling Scrabble tiles) and the point that external images can be reinterpreted while mental images cannot (Chambers and Reisberg).
numbers: Burst of rotations 800 to 1800 ms after zoid entry; external rotation 150 to 200 ms vs internal 1000 to 1800 ms (the 1994 paper said 800 to 1200 ms). Chambers and Reisberg: no subject found ambiguity in an image; 100% could reinterpret their own drawing.
quote: Computational steps are not actually eliminated; they are offloaded from the agent to the world.
limits: Review article; the Tetris figures are quoted from forthcoming work and differ from the final 1994 text.
agent_relevance: The reinterpretation result is the best argument for writing a hypothesis down (code, table) so it can be re-read in a new way, not only held in context.

source: Kirsh (2010) Thinking with external representations (AI & Society 25)
finding: Asks why people interact with a representation when the environment holds nothing that could not be inferred in principle. Lists seven functions: change the cost structure of inference, shareable object of thought, persistent referents, re-representation, more natural structure, more explicit encoding, building arbitrarily complex structure, and lower cost of controlling thought.
numbers: No single experiment; cites Kirsh and Maglio 1994 for Tetris, noting physical rotation is faster and less error prone than mental rotation.
limits: A conceptual synthesis; goes beyond 'offloading memory' without a new quantified test.
agent_relevance: Nearest account of why an LLM that already 'could' reason in text still gains from running tools: cost structure and re-representation, not new facts.

source: Kirsh (2013) Thinking with the body (marking in dance)
finding: Ethnography of dancers who 'mark' a phrase (do it partly) and thereby think about it. Argues marking is a lower-cost vehicle that anchors mental projection and can be better than imagination alone.
numbers: Qualitative; no sample statistics extracted. Conditions named: projection (subjects see moves), imagination (blank page).
limits: Ethnographic; interpretations not independently coded in the part I read; year approximate.
agent_relevance: Cheaper partial versions of an action (dry run, stub, sketch) can help thinking; echoes a toy-input probe before a full attempt.

source: Maglio, Matlock, Raphaely, Chernicky & Kirsh (1999) Interactive skill in Scrabble (CogSci 21)
finding: Follow-up by the same group applying epistemic action to Scrabble tile rearranging. Only Crossref bibliographic metadata was seen; the paper text was not retrieved.
limits: Not read; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Check the paper for human data on rearranging tiles as a cue to word search.

source: Maglio et al. (1997) Beyond embodiment: cognition as interactive skill (Behavioral and Brain Sciences)
finding: Commentary extending the interactive skill view. Only Crossref metadata seen; text not read.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Not used for claims.

source: Friston et al. (2015) Active inference and epistemic value (Cognitive Neuroscience)
finding: Formal counterpart: expected free energy of a policy splits into extrinsic value (expected utility toward goals) and epistemic value (expected information gain). Epistemic value is maximised until no more information can be gained, then exploitation follows. Seen via the Europe PMC abstract only.
numbers: Abstract only; simulations mentioned include precision updates resembling dopamine discharge. No other numbers read.
quote: Epistemic value is maximized until there is no further information gain, after which exploitation is assured
limits: Abstract only (not open access); linking it to Kirsh and Maglio's 1994 definition is my reading, not a claim the abstract makes.
agent_relevance: A principled stopping rule: probe while expected information gain is positive, then commit. Same shape as our G1 and G6.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models (ICLR)
finding: Interleaving thoughts with actions (search, environment steps) lets the LLM gather facts before answering. Acting grounds reasoning; without it chain of thought hallucinates.
numbers: ALFWorld: best ReAct trial 71% vs best Act-only 45% vs BUTLER 37%; worst ReAct trial (48%) beat both. Relative gain over Act 33 to 90%, mean 62% over 6 trials. WebShop success rate: ReAct 40.0 vs Act 30.1, IL 29.1, IL+RL 28.7, human expert 59.6. HotpotQA failure analysis: hallucination 0% of ReAct failures vs 56% of CoT failures; ReAct reasoning errors 47%, empty search results 23%.
limits: Prompting only, 2022 models (PaLM, GPT-3); ReAct's actions are mostly information gathering from a search tool, which is only partly the same as probing one's own work. Few-shot, hand-written prompts.
agent_relevance: Closest AI test of acting to reveal information. Shows the value, and a failure mode: repeated or uninformative actions (reasoning errors 47% of failures).

source: Li, Kim & Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Tests whether a model picks the one question that makes an underspecified problem solvable. Models are good at the math versions but weak at logic and planning. Solving the fully specified version does not imply asking the right question.
numbers: GSM-Q and GSME-Q above 80% accuracy; Logic-Q and Planning-Q under 50% (abstract: 40 to 50%). Multiple-choice question selection.
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Choosing among given options, not open-ended; one missing variable only.
agent_relevance: Warns that an LLM cannot be trusted to choose its own most informative probe. Select the probe in code (G5) where possible.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang & Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: LLMs placed as bandit agents rarely explore well without help. Only GPT-4 with chain of thought and an externally computed summary of history explored satisfactorily.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2, many prompts. Basic GPT-4 prompt: T=500 rounds, 20 replicates, more than 60% of replicates chose the best arm only a handful of times (suffix failure, like greedy).
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Simple multi-armed bandits, 2023-24 models; newer models not tested in the version read.
agent_relevance: Probing for information is not automatic in LLMs; a scaffold must force or structure it, and summarise results in code rather than leave raw history.

source: Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs (arXiv 2402.03271)
finding: Chooses which question to ask by simulating answers and scoring each question by expected information gain, then propagating scores through a tree. Directly formalises 'ask the most informative probe'.
numbers: Average gain 38.1% in task success over direct prompting across models, 5 datasets; DX medical dataset 97.0% with GPT-4; MedDG 81.4% (Gemini-1.5-Pro) and 88.0% (GPT-4); troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3%; beats CoT-SC by 33.8% and Reflexion by 29.9% on average.
limits: Simplified simulated settings (20 Questions, simplified diagnosis); answers come from a scripted respondent; baselines chosen by the authors; author list not captured.
agent_relevance: An information-gain probe selector is feasible in code; shows measurable benefit when the information gap is clear.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: agent-computer interfaces enable automated software engineering
finding: Interface design for exploration matters. A purpose-built search, file viewer and edit-with-lint interface raised resolve rates versus a plain shell. Agents' exploration by chains of cd, ls, cat was inefficient.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo: 12.47% (286 of 2,294) on SWE-bench full, 18.00% (54 of 300) on Lite; 64% relative increase over shell-only; 6.7x RAG on Lite at 8 to 13x cost; HumanEvalFix 88.3%.
limits: Cost per instance capped at $4; gains confounded across interface features; 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Which observations the tool returns (a compact viewer vs raw cat) decides how useful a probe is.

source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli & Zhou (2024) Teaching large language models to self-debug (ICLR)
finding: Execution results and the model's own explanation of its code serve as probes. The model improves after seeing what the program actually did.
numbers: Spider +2 to 3% (hardest level +9%) without tests; TransCoder and MBPP up to +12% with unit tests (about +12% TransCoder, +8% MBPP for Codex); matches or beats baselines that sample more than 10x candidates; 60 to 70% of successful fixes address output mismatch (TransCoder and MBPP).
limits: Test-case feedback relies on tests being available; effects vary by backbone model.
agent_relevance: Supports 'run it, read the real output, then revise' (G2). The probe is the execution trace.
